meta.base_text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC, Hebrew and Aramaic)

preamble.summary: The Greek tradition preserves two distinct books covering the Ezra-Nehemiah material. Esdras A (1 Esdras in English) is a free-form Greek narrative paraphrasing and reshaping material from 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra, and Nehemiah 7–8 with a unique added narrative — the Story of the Three Youths at the court of Darius. Esdras B translates MT Ezra-Nehemiah more literally and is the source of modern English 'Ezra' and 'Nehemiah' as two separate books. This file documents the Esdras B tradition's rendering choices; the larger 1 Esdras question is a separate tradition-layer issue.
preamble.notable_variants: The Cyrus decree at 1:1–2 whose Greek wording parallels 2 Chronicles 36:23 and sets up the Persian-period return; the 'skilled scribe' formula at 7:6 (grammateus tachys) that supplies NT scribe-vocabulary; the communal confession at 9:6–7 whose posture and language shape Hellenistic Jewish penitential liturgy; and the handling of the Aramaic sections of the Hebrew-Aramaic text (Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26) where the LXX translates from Aramaic without marking the language shift.
preamble.theological_legacy: The 1 Esdras / Esdras A tradition shaped Hellenistic and early Christian readings of the Persian-period return by adding the Story of the Three Youths, with its famous 'truth is the greatest' speech (1 Esdras 4:41) — a text cited in patristic literature as a Greek biblical source for reflection on truth. Esdras B preserved the more sober historiography that the MT and Western canon inherit.

renderings.mt_rendering: the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia
renderings.lxx_rendering: the Lord roused the spirit of Cyrus
notes: The LXX's exēgeiren ('roused, awakened') is the verb used for resurrection in the NT (1 Cor 6:14, Rom 8:11). The divine-rousing-of-the-spirit vocabulary in LXX historical books (here, and at Haggai 1:14, Zech 4:1) carries a resonance that Greek Christian readers found naturally applicable to the resurrection and to the awakening of the believer's spirit.

Ezra 1:1 is quoted almost verbatim from the closing verse of 2 Chronicles — the same Cyrus decree. The Hebrew canon's order placed Chronicles last and Ezra separately; in either order, the repetition creates a strong narrative link between the end of the exile and the beginning of restoration.

renderings.mt_reading: יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם נָתַן לִי הָאָרֶץ
renderings.lxx_reading: κύριος ὁ θεὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἔδωκέν μοι πάσας τὰς βασιλείας τῆς γῆς
renderings.mt_rendering: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth
renderings.lxx_rendering: The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth
notes: The 'God of heaven' (theos tou ouranou) is a standard Persian-period divine title in the Aramaic documents of Ezra and Nehemiah, and the LXX preserves it. The title reappears in Revelation 11:13 ('they … gave glory to the God of heaven'), where the LXX-Ezra language frames a universal acknowledgment scene.

The imperial-authority-given-by-God framing of Cyrus's decree shaped Jewish understanding of legitimate gentile rulers (Isaiah's call of Cyrus at 45:1 as mashiach; Paul's Rom 13:1 submission to governing authorities).

renderings.mt_rendering: a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses
renderings.lxx_rendering: a swift scribe in the Law of Moses
notes: The Hebrew mahir ('skilled, quick') is rendered as tachys ('swift'). The title grammateus tachys became an honorific for the learned scribe in Hellenistic Jewish usage.

The NT's grammateis ('scribes') in the Gospels are the institutional descendants of this Ezra-type. Ezra's characterization as the archetypal scribe skilled in the Law shapes the Gospel's portrayal of the scribal class — sometimes with respect (the scribe of Mark 12:34, 'not far from the kingdom'), sometimes polemically (Matthew 23's woes).

renderings.mt_reading: עֲוֺנֹתֵינוּ רָבוּ לְמַעְלָה רֹאשׁ וְאַשְׁמָתֵנוּ גָדְלָה עַד לַשָּׁמָיִם
renderings.lxx_reading: αἱ ἀνομίαι ἡμῶν ἐπληθύνθησαν ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς ἡμῶν καὶ αἱ πλημμέλειαι ἡμῶν ἐμεγαλύνθησαν ἕως εἰς οὐρανόν
renderings.mt_rendering: our iniquities have risen over our heads and our guilt has grown up to the heavens
renderings.lxx_rendering: our lawlessnesses have multiplied above our heads and our offenses have grown up to heaven
notes: The LXX's anomiai ('lawlessnesses') renders Hebrew avonot — a key LXX equivalence that supplies NT vocabulary. 1 John 3:4 defines sin as anomia, 'lawlessness,' deploying the standard LXX term.

The 'guilt growing up to heaven' image reappears at Revelation 18:5 ('her sins have piled up to heaven'), where the Babylon-judgment scene explicitly echoes LXX Ezra's vocabulary of cumulative corporate guilt. Revelation 18 reads Babylon through LXX-Ezra eyes.
Ezra's communal confession posture (kneeling, hands spread, weeping) became the template for Hellenistic Jewish and early Christian public penitential prayer.
